section.title: Database — SQL vs JDBC
section.subtitle: Tables, keys, CRUD queries, joins, aggregates, relationships, indexes and transactions. Python uses sqlite3; Java uses JDBC.

topics.title: Database Creation
topics.learn: Creating a database and connecting to it.

python.definition: sqlite3.connect() creates/opens a .db file — no server needed. For MySQL/Postgres use mysql-connector or psycopg2.
python.code:
import sqlite3

# Creates students.db if missing
conn = sqlite3.connect("students.db")
cursor = conn.cursor()

# For MySQL:
# import mysql.connector
# conn = mysql.connector.connect(host="localhost", user="root", password="pw", database="school")

java.definition: JDBC connects via DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password) using a database driver jar (mysql-connector-j, postgresql).

python.definition: CREATE TABLE defines columns with data types (INTEGER, TEXT, REAL) and constraints. execute() runs SQL; commit() saves changes.
python.code:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect("school.db")
c = conn.cursor()

c.execute("""CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS students (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    age INTEGER,
    marks REAL
)""")
conn.commit()

java.definition: Same SQL via Statement.execute() or PreparedStatement. Column types map to SQL types (INT, VARCHAR, DOUBLE).

topics.title: Primary Key & Foreign Key
topics.learn: Constraints that identify rows and link tables.

python.definition: PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each row. FOREIGN KEY links a column to another table's primary key, enforcing referential integrity.
python.code:
c.execute("""CREATE TABLE courses (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT,
    student_id INTEGER,
    FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id)
)""")
conn.commit()

java.definition: Identical SQL — JDBC just sends the statement to the database engine.

python.definition: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE modifies, DELETE removes — always parameterised (?) to prevent SQL injection. commit() persists changes.
python.code:
# INSERT
c.execute("INSERT INTO students (name, age, marks) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
          ("Priya", 20, 91.5))

# UPDATE
c.execute("UPDATE students SET marks = ? WHERE name = ?", (95.0, "Priya"))

# DELETE
c.execute("DELETE FROM students WHERE age < ?", (18,))
conn.commit()

java.definition: PreparedStatement with ? placeholders — safer than string concatenation. executeUpdate() returns rows affected.

python.definition: SELECT retrieves rows; WHERE filters. fetchall() returns all rows, fetchone() a single row.
python.code:
# All students
c.execute("SELECT * FROM students")
all_rows = c.fetchall()

# With filter
c.execute("SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > ?", (80,))
 toppers = c.fetchall()

for row in toppers:
    print(row)

java.definition: ResultSet iterates query results row by row; getString()/getInt() read columns.

python.definition: ORDER BY sorts ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC). GROUP BY aggregates rows per group — used with COUNT, SUM etc.
python.code:
# Sort by marks descending
c.execute("SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC")

# Group: average marks per course
c.execute("""SELECT course_id, AVG(marks), COUNT(*)
             FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id""")
for row in c.fetchall():
    print(row)

java.definition: Same SQL clauses; ResultSet rows come pre-sorted/grouped by the database.

python.definition: JOIN merges rows from tables on a related key. INNER JOIN keeps matches; LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows.
python.code:
c.execute("""SELECT students.name, courses.title
             FROM students
             JOIN enrollments ON students.id = enrollments.student_id
             JOIN courses ON courses.id = enrollments.course_id""")
for row in c.fetchall():
    print(row)

java.definition: Identical JOIN SQL executed through JDBC.

python.definition: Aggregate functions compute a single value over rows: COUNT(*), SUM(col), AVG(col), MIN(col), MAX(col).
python.code:
c.execute("""SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(marks), MIN(marks), MAX(marks)
             FROM students""")
count, avg, mn, mx = c.fetchone()
print(f"Students: {count}, Avg: {avg:.1f}")

java.definition: Same aggregate SQL; read results via ResultSet getters.

python.definition: 1-to-many: FK on the 'many' side. Many-to-many: a junction table with two FKs.
python.code:
# 1-to-many: course has many students
# students.course_id -> courses.id

# many-to-many: students <-> tags via junction
c.execute("""CREATE TABLE student_tags (
    student_id INTEGER,
    tag_id INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, tag_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id),
    FOREIGN KEY (tag_id) REFERENCES tags(id)
)""")
conn.commit()

java.definition: Same relational design — JDBC only executes the DDL.
java.code:
stmt.executeUpdate("""CREATE TABLE student_tags (
    student_id INTEGER,
    tag_id INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, tag_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES students(id),
    FOREIGN KEY (tag_id) REFERENCES tags(id)
)""");

python.definition: CREATE INDEX speeds up lookups. Transactions group statements — conn.commit() saves all, conn.rollback() undoes on error.
python.code:
c.execute("CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_name ON students(name)")
conn.commit()

# Transaction
try:
    c.execute("INSERT INTO students VALUES (?,?,?,?)", (1, "A", 20, 90))
    c.execute("INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (?,?)", (1, 1))
    conn.commit()          # both succeed together
except Exception:
    conn.rollback()        # undo all

java.definition: conn.setAutoCommit(false) starts a transaction; commit()/rollback() control it. Same CREATE INDEX SQL.
